$comment: A LANGUAGE prior. Data only, no code. Staged here for transfer to eoPriors; nothing in packages/ may hardcode any of it.

provenance.source: English Wikipedia, 'African-American Vernacular English' and 'Ain't' articles, fetched 2026-08-19, quoted directly: "AAVE... employs ain't as a general negative marker" that can substitute for "am not, isn't, aren't, haven't, and hasn't," and some speakers use it "instead of don't, doesn't, or didn't" (example: "I ain't know that"). Corroborated by Jack Sidnell, 'Outline of AAVE Grammar' (2002), and by real occurrence counts in a genuine CORAAL-derived transcript sample (147 lines containing 'ain't' in a 4,454-row sample, Koenecke et al. 2020 PNAS reproducibility data).
provenance.built_by: hand-curated from cited sources plus real transcript evidence, deliberately minimal rather than padded with recalled-but-uncited items

attested.period: NOT one snapshot — the pooled CORAAL evidence this file cites spans two materially different calendar periods. DCB (Washington DC): recorded July 2015 - December 2017. ROC (Rochester NY): recorded 2016-2017 (Sharese King's dissertation fieldwork). PRV (Princeville NC): recorded August 2003 - June 2004 (Rowe, Wolfram et al., NC Language and Life Project) - roughly 12-13 years earlier than DCB/ROC, from a different community. 'ain't' as measured against this file's own real-material evidence is therefore two temporally separated samples, not a single contemporary reading. A genuine real-time TREND study of DC AAE does exist in the literature (DCA, 1968-1969, paired with DCB 2015-2017 by Arnson/Kendall/Farrington's ongoing work) but DCA is NOT present in either local corpus this file or its companion eval draws on - confirmed absent from live_priors' coraal-manifest.json and from the-fold's eval/corpus/coraal-transcripts.csv (whose 'source' column holds only DCB/PRV/ROC).
attested.basis: Grounded 2026-08-19 via https://oraal.github.io/coraal-components (fetched directly, exact date ranges quoted), cross-checked against local files (live_priors/manifests/coraal-manifest.json; per-transcript header lines confirming the CSV's 'age' field is speaker age AT RECORDING, not a calendar year — neither the manifest, the .txt files, nor the CSV carry a calendar recording date anywhere locally; the ranges above come entirely from the external CORAAL-components fetch). DCA/trend-study framing via WebSearch of Arnson/Kendall/Farrington's 'Twentieth Century Sound Change in Washington DC African American English' project — not independently fetched in full.
attested.confidence: high for the DCB/PRV/ROC date ranges (directly quoted from CORAAL's own components page); medium for the DCA trend-study framing (secondhand)

region.detail: NOT geographically/functionally uniform, and the non-uniformity is a real, specific, documented FUNCTIONAL split, not just a frequency wobble. Sabriya Fisher (2022), 'The Status of ain't in Philadelphia African American English' (Language Variation and Change 34(1)), a real corpus study of 42 African-American Philadelphians plus Southern-born comparison speakers: past/perfective 'ain't' - EXACTLY this file's own diagnostic example, 'I ain't know that' = 'I didn't know that' - is a relatively RECENT innovation that has been increasing specifically among Philadelphia (Northern) speakers, while Southern-born speakers in the same corpus use it markedly less regardless of age; for ain't's more established copula/auxiliary functions (isn't/aren't/haven't), the pattern REVERSES - Philadelphia speakers disfavor ain't there compared to Southern speakers. This file's single flat 'ain't' entry cannot distinguish these two functions (the negationWords mechanism is purely lexical, not grammatical-function-aware) - a real, disclosed limitation, not fixed here. A direct measurement against this repo's own staged material (case-insensitive word-boundary count over the 4,450-row eval/corpus/coraal-transcripts.csv, grouped by the 'source' region column) found DCB=1.07/1000 words, PRV=0.535/1000 words, ROC=0.209/1000 words - a real ~5x DCB-vs-ROC spread - but this is reported as SUGGESTIVE, not confirmatory: per-speaker counts are extremely skewed (2 of 39 DCB speakers account for 86 of 149 total DCB hits), the sample is small, and the ranking does not cleanly match Fisher's North>South framing (ROC is also Northern but lowest here) - explicitly not asserted as a validated regional ranking.
region.basis: Sabriya Fisher (2022), Language Variation and Change 34(1), https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language-variation-and-change/article/status-of-aint-in-philadelphia-african-american-english/297B3E7281632D5E268222D9CF3F4437 (author/venue independently confirmed by a second search). Direct measurement: live computation over the-fold's eval/corpus/coraal-transcripts.csv (4,450 rows), grouped by its 'source' column (DCB/PRV/ROC) and cross-checked per-speaker via 'basefile' for the skew finding. A secondary dialect-density claim (Johnson et al. 2022, Interspeech) was found via search summary only and could NOT be independently verified (PDF unreadable in this environment) - not relied on for the conclusion above, named only as directionally consistent.

notes: 'en-AAVE' is a DESCRIPTIVE LABEL, not a registered BCP-47 language/variant subtag -- there is no formal IETF-registered code for African American Vernacular English at the time this file was written, and this file does not pretend otherwise.

negation: this list holds ONLY what AAVE adds beyond Standard English's own NEGATION_WORDS (priors.js, giver lang/en) -- 'not', 'never', 'don't', etc. are already covered there and are not repeated here. A caller wanting BOTH must union this file's `negation` array with lang/en.json's own set (this file is additive, not a replacement).

'ain't' is the one addition: a general preverbal negator that, in AAVE, reaches into past-tense and habitual slots Standard English's own 'ain't' (where it exists at all, as an informal contraction of 'am not'/'isn't'/'aren't'/'haven't'/'hasn't') does not cover -- 'I ain't know that' (= 'I didn't know that') is the diagnostic example both cited sources give.

Negative concord (multiple negation within one clause co-referring to a single negative meaning, e.g. 'They didn't have no books') is DELIBERATELY NOT represented as additional trigger words here: it is a co-occurrence PATTERN on the SAME existing negators (ain't/don't/didn't/never), never a new negation-bearing word. Verified directly against real transcript data (not just asserted): every 'nobody'/'nothing' occurrence found alongside a negator in the real CORAAL-derived sample checked here had an explicit co-present auxiliary negator (ain't/don't/can't) -- 'nobody'/'nothing' never carried negation alone, the same exclusion Standard English's own NEGATION_WORDS list already makes.

DISCLOSED STRUCTURAL LIMIT, found while researching this file rather than glossed over: AAVE's negative-inversion construction fronts the negator+auxiliary before the subject ('Can't nobody afford that' = 'Nobody can afford that') -- here the negation trigger sits BEFORE the subject, not immediately before the finite verb the way this mechanism's before-the-verb window assumes. Adding 'ain't'/'can't' to the vocabulary does not by itself fix this: the window's own adjacency assumption is what would need to change to catch negative-inversion sentences, a larger, unattempted change here.

Consumed by perceiver/text/relations.js::discoverRelationVocab and ::extractRelations via the injected `negationWords` option (a Set) -- the same seam bin/priors/lang/en.json's own abbreviations already opened, and bin/priors/lang/eu.json (Basque) and bin/priors/lang/pcm.json (Nigerian Pidgin) already use.

Measured against real material: eval/vendored-prior-eval.md in the-fold repo records the before/after result of injecting this file's `negation` set (unioned with lang/en.json's own) against real CORAAL-derived transcript text (Koenecke et al. 2020 PNAS reproducibility data, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, research use -- kept local, not redistributed in either repo).

Added 2026-08-19 (schema NegationPrior@2): the `attested`/`region` blocks above are the grounded answer to 'chronologically stamped, regional when possible' -- and the finding sharpens note 3 above rather than merely adding metadata around it. This file's own diagnostic example ('I ain't know that') is EXACTLY the past/perfective use Fisher (2022) documents as a recent, Northern-city-concentrated innovation, not a stable pan-AAVE fact -- so the earlier phrasing 'a general preverbal negator that, in AAVE, reaches into past-tense and habitual slots' was itself overclaiming uniformity the cited literature does not support. Left as originally written above (not rewritten) so the record shows what was claimed before this grounding pass and what was found after; the honest current state is `region.scope: regional-variation-documented`, not the flat universality note 3 implies.
